lessons.title: Context: British Empire & Indian Immigration
lessons.description: Victorian Empire, Indian immigration, and the historical world Gupta dramatises in The Empress.
lessons.content_html:
The British Empire and India

Tanika Gupta’s The Empress (2013) is set in Victorian Britain during the height of the British Empire. By the mid-nineteenth century, India was Britain’s most valuable colony — often called the “jewel in the crown.” The play dramatises the real experiences of Indian people who came to Britain as workers, servants, and political activists, exploring how they were treated in a society that profited enormously from their labour while viewing them as racially inferior.

Understanding this historical context is essential for the Edexcel exam. AO3 requires you to show how the play’s meaning is shaped by the context in which it was written and set. Gupta wrote The Empress in 2013, but set it in the 1880s–1890s to draw parallels between Victorian racism and modern attitudes towards immigration.

Key Fact

In 1876, Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India — the title that gives the play its name. This was a political act designed to tighten Britain’s control over India after the 1857 rebellion. The title symbolises the power imbalance at the heart of the play.

Ayahs: Indian Nannies in Britain

One of the most important groups in the play is the ayahs — Indian women employed as nursemaids by British families travelling between India and England. Ayahs were hired for the voyage to care for British children, but many were abandoned in London once they arrived. Without money, language skills, or legal rights, they were left destitute in a foreign country. Gupta based this on real historical records from the Ayahs’ Home, a shelter established in the East End of London in 1891 to help stranded Indian women.

The real Ayahs’ Home was established in Hackney, East London, by the London City Mission. It provided temporary shelter for Indian women who had been brought to England and then abandoned by their employers. Records show that hundreds of women passed through the home. Gupta uses this as a central location in the play, making the audience confront the human cost of Empire. The ayahs’ vulnerability highlights the power imbalance between British employers and Indian servants — they could be discarded like unwanted luggage once they were no longer useful.

Lascars: Indian Sailors

The play also features lascars — Indian sailors who crewed British merchant ships. Lascars made up a significant proportion of the British merchant navy by the 1880s, yet they were paid far less than white sailors, housed in the worst quarters, and had no legal protection if they were abandoned at port. Many ended up destitute in London’s docklands. Gupta uses the character of Hari to represent their exploitation.

Key Fact

Gupta draws on real historical sources — the Ayahs’ Home records, lascar testimonies, and the political career of Dadabhai Naoroji — to create a play that is both a historical drama and a commentary on modern immigration and racism. The examiner will reward students who can explain how Gupta uses historical context to make a contemporary argument.

Racism in Victorian Britain

Victorian Britain presented a contradiction. The Empire was celebrated as a civilising mission, yet Indian people who came to Britain were treated with suspicion, contempt, and open racism. Scientific racism — the idea that white Europeans were biologically superior — was widely accepted in the Victorian era. This ideology underpinned the entire colonial project and is reflected in the attitudes of characters like Mrs Phelps in the play.

Queen Victoria never appears on stage in The Empress, but her presence looms over the entire play. She is the ultimate symbol of imperial power — distant, untouchable, and indifferent to the suffering of her Indian subjects. The title “Empress of India” was granted by the Royal Titles Act of 1876, partly at the urging of Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli, to consolidate British authority after the 1857 Indian rebellion. For the characters in the play, Victoria represents both the promise and the betrayal of Empire: a ruler who claims to protect all her subjects but whose system exploits and abandons them.

Gupta’s choice to keep Victoria offstage is deliberate. It mirrors how the powerful remain invisible while the powerless bear the consequences of their decisions — a structural choice that reinforces the play’s themes of inequality and absence of justice.

Why Gupta Wrote The Empress

Tanika Gupta is a British-Bengali playwright whose work frequently explores the experiences of South Asian communities in Britain. She wrote The Empress because she felt that the stories of Indian people in Victorian Britain had been erased from history. The play was commissioned by the Royal Shakespeare Company and first performed in 2013. Gupta wanted to show that immigration is not a modern phenomenon — Indian people have been part of British society for centuries, yet their contributions have been overlooked and their suffering ignored.

This authorial intent is directly relevant to AO3. Gupta is not just writing a historical play — she is making an argument about how Britain remembers (and forgets) its imperial past. The examiner will reward students who can connect Gupta’s choices as a playwright to her broader political purpose.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Edexcel Component 1 Section B, you must write about the whole play, not just an extract. Context (AO3) should be woven into your analysis, not bolted on as a separate paragraph. When discussing the ayahs or lascars, link their fictional experiences to the real historical conditions Gupta dramatises. Strong answers use phrases like “Gupta uses the historical reality of the Ayahs’ Home to expose...” rather than simply stating background facts.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The play is set during the height of the British Empire in the 1880s–1890s, when India was under direct Crown rule and Queen Victoria held the title Empress of India.
  • Gupta dramatises the real experiences of ayahs (Indian nannies abandoned in London) and lascars (Indian sailors exploited on British ships) to expose the human cost of Empire.
  • Understanding Gupta’s purpose — recovering erased histories and drawing parallels with modern immigration — is essential for AO3 in the exam.

lessons.title: Act 1: Arrival & Hope
lessons.description: Rani and Abdul arrive in London as Gupta establishes hope, vulnerability, and Victorian prejudice.
lessons.content_html:
Act 1: A World of Hope and Danger

Act 1 of The Empress introduces the play’s central characters as they arrive in London, each carrying their own hopes and expectations. Gupta uses their arrival to dramatise the contrast between the promise of Britain and the harsh reality that awaits Indian immigrants. For the exam, you need to analyse how Gupta establishes character, setting, and theme in this opening act — particularly through the dramatic irony of characters who believe Britain will treat them fairly.

The Arrivals: Rani, Abdul Karim, and the Voyage

Rani is a young ayah who arrives in London having cared for a British family’s children during the voyage from India. She is hopeful and curious about England, seeing it as a land of opportunity. She also shares the voyage with Abdul Karim — though they have separate storylines. Abdul Karim is a historical figure sent to Queen Victoria as a Golden Jubilee gift; he becomes her Munshi (language tutor). Rani’s own romantic storyline involves Hari, a lascar sailor she meets on the ship. Gupta presents their arrival with warmth and energy — they marvel at London’s size, its buildings, and its bustling streets. This initial excitement is crucial because it sets up the audience for the disappointment and exploitation that follows.

The audience, knowing the historical reality of how ayahs were treated, experiences dramatic irony throughout these early scenes. Rani’s hope makes her later abandonment more devastating. Gupta deliberately builds sympathy before introducing the cruelty of the system.

Key Fact

Gupta presents Rani and Abdul as hopeful and trusting when they first arrive in London. This optimism creates dramatic irony because the audience knows the system will exploit them. The contrast between hope and reality is one of the play’s central dramatic devices.

The Ayahs’ Experiences

Alongside Rani, the play introduces other ayahs who have been stranded in London. These women share stories of being hired in India, promised return passages, and then abandoned once their employers no longer needed them. Gupta uses their collective testimony to build a picture of systemic exploitation — this is not one bad employer but an entire system that treats Indian women as disposable.

The ayahs function both as individual characters and as a collective voice. When they share their stories of abandonment, Gupta creates a cumulative effect — each story reinforces the last, building a damning picture of how the Empire treated Indian women. This technique prevents the audience from dismissing Rani’s experience as an isolated case. The collective testimony makes clear that exploitation is the norm, not the exception.

This choral quality also connects the play to the tradition of political theatre, where individual stories represent broader social injustice. Gupta is not just telling Rani’s story — she is telling the story of hundreds of real women whose experiences were erased from history.

Hari the Lascar

Hari is introduced in Act 1 as a young Indian sailor — a lascar — working on British merchant ships. His experiences contrast with the ayahs’ in important ways. While the ayahs are exploited through abandonment, Hari faces exploitation through brutal working conditions: low pay, dangerous work, and racial abuse from white sailors. Gupta uses Hari to show that Indian men and women faced different but equally devastating forms of discrimination.

Hari is also politically aware in ways that Rani initially is not. He begins to question the fairness of the system, making him an important voice for resistance that will develop further in Act 2. Gupta uses Hari to introduce the idea that exploitation breeds political consciousness.

Key Fact

Gupta uses Hari to show a different kind of exploitation from the ayahs. While the ayahs are abandoned by employers, Hari is actively abused as a worker. Together, they represent the breadth of how the Empire exploited Indian people across gender and occupation.

Victorian Attitudes to Indian Servants

Act 1 also establishes the attitudes of British characters towards their Indian servants. Mrs Phelps, a British woman, treats the ayahs with a mixture of condescension and casual cruelty. She views them as useful but fundamentally inferior — objects to be used and discarded. Gupta presents Victorian paternalism through Mrs Phelps: the belief that British people were doing Indians a favour by employing them, while simultaneously denying them any rights or dignity.

Gupta layers dramatic irony throughout Act 1. The audience sees Rani’s excitement about London while already knowing (from the play’s context and the other ayahs’ stories) that her trust will be betrayed. This is a deliberate structural choice: Gupta wants the audience to feel the injustice before the characters fully understand it. The gap between Rani’s hope and the audience’s knowledge creates emotional tension that builds throughout the act.

The dramatic irony also functions as a comment on the Empire itself. Just as Rani believes in the promise of Britain, millions of colonised people were told that British rule would benefit them. The play dramatises the moment when that promise is revealed as a lie.

By the end of Act 1, Gupta has established the key dynamics: hope versus reality, exploitation versus resistance, and the power imbalance between British employers and Indian workers. The act ends with the audience fully invested in the characters’ fates, aware that the system is stacked against them.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about Act 1, always link character presentation to Gupta’s dramatic purpose. Don’t just describe what happens — analyse why Gupta chose to present it this way. For AO4, consider alternative interpretations: is Rani naive, or does her hope represent a universal human quality that the audience should admire? Strong answers explore multiple readings of the same moment.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Act 1 establishes hope and vulnerability through Rani and Abdul’s arrival in London, creating dramatic irony as the audience knows the system will betray them.
  • The ayahs function as a collective voice, building a cumulative picture of systemic exploitation rather than isolated incidents.
  • Hari the lascar introduces a male perspective on exploitation and the beginnings of political resistance, contrasting with Rani’s initial optimism.

lessons.title: Act 2: Exploitation & Resistance
lessons.description: How Gupta dramatises exploitation, abandonment, and growing resistance through the ayahs and Hari.
lessons.content_html:
Act 2: When Hope Turns to Hardship

Act 2 of The Empress is where Gupta shifts the play’s emotional register from hope to anger. The initial optimism of Act 1 gives way to a clear-eyed depiction of how the British Empire exploited Indian people. The ayahs discover they have been abandoned, Hari’s working conditions deteriorate further, and the shadow of the 1857 Indian rebellion looms over every interaction between Indian and British characters.

For the exam, Act 2 is crucial because it contains the play’s most powerful moments of dramatic injustice. Gupta wants the audience to feel outrage at the system, not just sympathy for individuals. Understanding how she builds this response is key to AO1 and AO4.

The Ayahs Abandoned

The central crisis of Act 2 is the moment when the ayahs realise they have been abandoned by their British employers. They were promised return passages to India, but no tickets arrive. They have no money, no legal rights, and no way of getting home. Gupta dramatises this moment with devastating simplicity — the women slowly understand that the promises were lies.

Key Fact

The ayahs’ abandonment is based on real historical records. Hundreds of Indian women were stranded in London after being brought to England by British families. Gupta uses this historical reality to show that the exploitation was not accidental — it was built into the system. The British employers knew they could abandon Indian women with no legal consequences.

The abandonment scene is structurally important because it marks the turning point of the play. Before this moment, there is still hope. After it, the characters must confront the reality of their situation and decide how to respond — with resignation or resistance.

Hari’s Working Conditions

While the ayahs face abandonment, Hari faces a different kind of exploitation. As a lascar, he works in brutal conditions: long hours, dangerous cargo, racial abuse from white sailors, and pay that is a fraction of what British crew members receive. Gupta uses Hari’s story to show that exploitation was not just about neglect but about active, deliberate injustice.

Historically, lascars were paid roughly one-fifth of what white sailors earned for the same work. They were housed in the worst quarters on ships, given inferior food, and had no legal protection if they were injured or abandoned at port. By the 1880s, lascars made up around a quarter of the British merchant navy — they were essential to the Empire’s trade, yet treated as expendable. Gupta draws directly on these records to create Hari’s experiences, ensuring the play’s depiction of exploitation is grounded in historical fact.

The exploitation gap — the vast difference between what lascars contributed to the Empire’s wealth and what they received in return — is central to Gupta’s argument. The Empire could not function without Indian labour, yet Indian workers were treated as less than human.

The Shadow of 1857

Gupta weaves the 1857 Indian Mutiny into Act 2 as a source of tension between Indian and British characters. British characters reference the rebellion to justify their suspicion and fear of Indians, arguing that they cannot be trusted with freedom or authority. Indian characters, by contrast, see 1857 as evidence that resistance is possible and necessary.

Key Fact

The 1857 Indian rebellion is never shown on stage, but it haunts Act 2 as a contested memory. British characters use it to justify their suspicion of Indian people, while Indian characters see it as a moment of resistance against injustice. Gupta uses this historical event to show how the same history can be interpreted in opposing ways depending on who holds power.

Growing Political Awareness

Act 2 marks a crucial shift as characters begin to move from suffering to resistance. Hari becomes increasingly politicised, questioning not just his own treatment but the entire structure of the Empire. He begins to articulate the argument that Indian people deserve equal rights — not charity, not paternalism, but justice. Gupta uses Hari’s growing political consciousness to move the play from personal stories of suffering towards a broader political argument.

Gupta structures Act 2 so that individual suffering leads naturally to collective action. The ayahs’ abandonment, Hari’s exploitation, and the memory of 1857 all converge to create a growing awareness that the problem is not individual cruelty but systemic injustice. This is a key dramatic choice: Gupta moves the play from melodrama (feeling sorry for victims) to political theatre (understanding and challenging the system that creates victims).

The transition from passive suffering to active resistance mirrors real historical patterns. Indian political movements in Britain grew from the shared experiences of workers, students, and intellectuals who recognised that their individual problems had structural causes. Gupta dramatises this awakening through Hari’s character arc.

By the end of Act 2, the play has moved from hope through exploitation to the beginnings of resistance. Gupta has established that the characters’ suffering is not random but structural, and that the only response is collective political action.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Act 2 is rich material for AO4 (evaluation). Consider alternative interpretations of key moments: is the ayahs’ abandonment a failure of individual employers or of the entire imperial system? Is Hari’s anger justified or dangerous? The examiner rewards students who can hold multiple interpretations simultaneously, using phrases like “while one reading suggests… an alternative interpretation is that…”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Act 2 marks the turning point from hope to exploitation, as the ayahs are abandoned and Hari faces worsening conditions.
  • The 1857 Indian rebellion functions as a contested memory — British characters use it to justify racism, while Indian characters see it as proof that resistance is possible.
  • Gupta moves the play from personal suffering to political awareness, using Hari’s growing consciousness to shift from melodrama to political theatre.

lessons.title: Act 3: The Empress & Resolution
lessons.description: Victoria's proclamation, Naoroji's election, and how the play resolves hope and disillusionment.
lessons.content_html:
Act 3: Power, Proclamation, and the Limits of Change

Act 3 of The Empress brings the play to its resolution, but Gupta deliberately avoids a simple happy ending. Instead, she presents a complex mixture of hope and disillusionment. Queen Victoria’s proclamation, the establishment of the Ayahs’ Home, and the historic election of Dadabhai Naoroji all suggest progress, but Gupta undercuts each moment to show that real change has not occurred.

For the exam, Act 3 is where AO4 (evaluation and alternative interpretations) becomes especially important. Is the ending hopeful or pessimistic? Does Gupta believe the system can change, or is she showing that progress is always incomplete? You need to be able to argue both sides.

Queen Victoria’s Proclamation

A key moment in Act 3 is the reference to Queen Victoria’s 1858 proclamation, which placed India under direct Crown rule following the 1857 rebellion. The proclamation promised that Indian subjects would be treated equally, that “none be in anywise favoured, none molested or disquieted, by reason of their religious faith or observances.” Gupta uses this historical document to create a devastating ironic contrast between the Empire’s promises and the characters’ lived reality.

Key Fact

Queen Victoria’s 1858 proclamation promised equality for all Indian subjects. Gupta sets this promise against the ayahs’ abandonment, Hari’s exploitation, and the racism faced by every Indian character. The gap between the proclamation’s words and the characters’ reality is one of the play’s most powerful dramatic effects.

The Ayahs’ Home

Act 3 depicts the establishment of the Ayahs’ Home as a moment of qualified hope. The home provides shelter and safety for the abandoned women, but Gupta presents it as a solution to a problem that should never have existed. The home is an act of charity within a system of exploitation — it helps individual women without challenging the structures that create their suffering.

Gupta makes an important distinction between charity and justice. The Ayahs’ Home is an act of charity — it helps women who have already been harmed. But Gupta implies that what Indian people need is not charity but justice: legal rights, equal pay, protection from exploitation, and an end to the racial hierarchy that treats them as inferior. This distinction is central to the play’s political argument and is worth exploring for AO4.

The Home also raises the question of who gets to define progress. From a British perspective, establishing the Home might seem generous and progressive. From the ayahs’ perspective, it is a bare minimum response to a catastrophic injustice. Gupta invites the audience to consider whose version of progress matters.

Dadabhai Naoroji’s Election

The play references the historic election of Dadabhai Naoroji as MP for Finsbury Central in 1892 — the first Asian person to be elected to the British Parliament. Gupta presents this as a moment of genuine hope: proof that Indian people could participate in the political system and challenge the Empire from within. Naoroji’s victory is celebrated by the Indian characters as a sign that change is possible.

However, Gupta also complicates this triumph. Naoroji won by a margin of just three votes, and his election was contested by opponents who used racist opposition. Lord Salisbury, the Conservative Prime Minister, said he doubted whether a British constituency would elect “a black man” (his Edinburgh speech, 1888). Hostile campaign opponents also used the term “fire-worshipper” (a reference to Naoroji’s Parsi faith) but this phrase is not Salisbury’s. Students should attribute “a black man” to Salisbury specifically. Gupta uses this to show that even when Indian people achieved success, they faced racism and resistance.

Key Fact

Dadabhai Naoroji was elected MP for Finsbury Central in 1892, the first Asian MP in British history. His election represents hope and political agency, but Gupta complicates this by showing the racist opposition he faced. The play presents progress as real but incomplete.

Hope and Disillusionment

The ending of The Empress is deliberately ambivalent. There are genuine moments of progress — the Ayahs’ Home, Naoroji’s election, the characters’ growing solidarity. But there is no sense that the fundamental injustice of the Empire has been resolved. Racism persists. Exploitation continues. The system remains intact, even if individuals find ways to survive within it.

Gupta avoids a happy ending because she is writing a political play, not a feel-good story. A neat resolution would suggest that the problems of Empire have been solved, which would be historically dishonest. By leaving the ending ambivalent, Gupta forces the audience to recognise that the issues the play raises — racism, exploitation, erased histories — are still relevant today. The play was written in 2013, during a period of intense debate about immigration in Britain. Gupta draws a direct line from Victorian attitudes to contemporary politics.

This refusal to provide closure is a deliberate dramatic choice. It mirrors the historical reality: there was no single moment when Indian people in Britain stopped facing discrimination. Progress was slow, uneven, and constantly challenged. Gupta’s ending reflects this truth.

The play’s final moments ask the audience to hold both hope and disillusionment simultaneously — to recognise that individuals can make a difference while acknowledging that the system they are fighting against is vast, deeply rooted, and slow to change.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Edexcel AO4, you must evaluate different interpretations. The ending of The Empress is ideal material for this. You could argue it is ultimately hopeful (Naoroji’s election, the Ayahs’ Home, characters’ solidarity) or ultimately pessimistic (racism persists, the system remains, charity replaces justice). The best answers hold both readings and explain why Gupta’s ambivalence is itself a deliberate choice.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Gupta uses Victoria’s proclamation of equality as an ironic contrast to the characters’ actual experiences of racism and exploitation.
  • Naoroji’s election as the first Asian MP represents real progress, but Gupta complicates it by showing the racist opposition he faced.
  • The ending is deliberately ambivalent — hope and disillusionment coexist, reflecting both historical reality and Gupta’s purpose of connecting Victorian and modern attitudes.

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.description: Analysing Rani, Abdul, Hari, Mrs Phelps, and Naoroji as vehicles for Gupta's themes.
lessons.content_html:
Characters as Vehicles for Theme

In The Empress, Gupta creates characters who are both individual human beings and representatives of broader historical experiences. For the Edexcel exam, you need to analyse characters on both levels: what they are like as people (AO1) and what they represent about the Empire, race, and power (AO3/AO4). This lesson examines the play’s five most important characters and how Gupta uses each to develop her themes.

Rani — Hope, Vulnerability, and Resilience

Rani is the emotional heart of the play. She arrives in London full of optimism and curiosity, making her a sympathetic figure from the start. Gupta uses Rani’s journey to dramatise the cycle of hope, betrayal, and resilience that defined the experience of many Indian women in Victorian Britain.

What makes Rani a compelling character is that she does not remain a passive victim. After her abandonment, she develops awareness of the system that has exploited her and finds strength in solidarity with the other ayahs. Her character arc moves from individual hope to collective resistance. Gupta presents Rani as resourceful and intelligent — the system fails her, not the other way round.

Key Fact

Rani’s character arc — from hope through betrayal to resilience — is the play’s emotional spine. Gupta uses her journey to show that the Empire’s victims were not passive: they suffered, they endured, and they found ways to resist. Rani’s resilience is political as well as personal.

Abdul — Loyalty and Quiet Strength

Abdul Karim represents a quieter form of resistance. (Note: Abdul Karim is not Rani’s husband — he has a separate storyline as Queen Victoria’s Munshi. Rani’s romantic partner is Hari the lascar.). Where Hari is vocal and politically active, Abdul demonstrates quiet strength — enduring hardship while protecting those around him. Gupta uses Abdul to show that resistance takes many forms, and that the everyday act of surviving in a hostile system is itself an act of courage.

Abdul also functions as a foil to Hari. Where Hari becomes increasingly angry and politicised, Abdul maintains a more pragmatic approach, focused on immediate survival. Gupta does not present either response as superior — both are understandable reactions to injustice.

The contrast between Abdul and Hari represents a real debate within colonised communities: is it better to work within the system or to challenge it directly? Abdul’s pragmatism keeps him and Rani alive, but it does not change the system. Hari’s anger drives political awareness, but it also puts him at risk. Gupta presents both approaches with sympathy, allowing the audience to evaluate them through AO4. This dual response mirrors historical reality — Indian communities in Victorian Britain contained both moderates and radicals.

Hari — Anger and Political Voice

Hari is the play’s most politically vocal character. As a lascar facing brutal working conditions, he develops from a frustrated worker into an articulate critic of the Empire. Gupta uses Hari to give voice to the argument that Indian people deserve not charity but equal rights and justice.

Hari’s character serves an important structural function. He connects the personal stories of exploitation to the broader political argument. Without Hari, the play would be a story of individual suffering; with him, it becomes a critique of an entire system. His growing political consciousness mirrors the historical development of Indian political movements in Britain.

Key Fact

Hari transforms the play from personal stories into political theatre. His anger is not random — it grows directly from his experience of exploitation. Gupta uses him to show that political consciousness emerges from lived injustice, not abstract ideology.

Mrs Phelps — Embodying Victorian Racism

Mrs Phelps is the play’s most prominent British character and the one who most clearly embodies Victorian attitudes towards Indian people. She is not a villain in the traditional sense — she does not set out to be cruel. Instead, her racism is casual, habitual, and built into her worldview. She genuinely believes she is being kind to the ayahs, even as she treats them as less than human.

Gupta’s most sophisticated choice with Mrs Phelps is making her racism ordinary rather than extreme. Mrs Phelps is not a cartoon villain — she is a recognisable type. Her condescension, her assumption of superiority, and her ability to discard Indian people without guilt are all presented as normal within Victorian society. This makes her more disturbing than an overtly cruel character would be, because it shows that racism does not require malice — it only requires a system that normalises inequality.

For AO4, consider whether Mrs Phelps is personally responsible for her attitudes, or whether she is simply a product of her society. Gupta seems to suggest both: Mrs Phelps is shaped by the system, but she also has the choice to see the ayahs as human beings, and she consistently fails to make that choice.

Dadabhai Naoroji — Working Within the System

Naoroji represents the possibility of using Britain’s own political system to challenge its injustices. His election as Britain’s first Asian MP in 1892 is the play’s most concrete symbol of hope. Gupta presents him as dignified, intelligent, and determined — a counter to the racist stereotypes applied to Indian people by characters like Mrs Phelps.

However, Gupta does not present Naoroji as a simple hero. His success is limited — one MP cannot dismantle an empire — and the racist opposition he faces (including Lord Salisbury’s contempt) shows that political progress is slow and contested. Naoroji represents the hope that the system can be changed from within, but Gupta leaves open the question of whether this hope is justified.

Queen Victoria appears on stage throughout the play as a significant speaking character. She is central to scenes with Abdul Karim, discussing Hindi lessons, the Empire, and royal authority. Her on-stage presence allows Gupta to dramatise power dynamics directly. Her title gives the play its name; her proclamation is referenced in Act 3; her empire creates the conditions that destroy the characters’ lives. Gupta’s decision to keep Victoria offstage is a deliberate structural choice. It mirrors how power operates: the most powerful people are often invisible, while the powerless bear the visible consequences of their decisions. Victoria’s absence is itself a form of dramatic commentary.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about characters for Edexcel, always connect them to Gupta’s dramatic purpose. Don’t just describe what characters do — explain why Gupta created them this way. Use the formula: “Gupta uses [character] to [dramatic purpose], which [effect on audience].” For AO4, offer alternative readings: is Mrs Phelps personally cruel or just a product of her society? Is Hari’s anger constructive or self-destructive?
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rani’s character arc from hope through betrayal to resilience represents the broader experience of Indian women exploited by the Empire.
  • Hari and Abdul represent contrasting responses to injustice — political activism versus pragmatic survival — and Gupta presents both with sympathy.
  • Mrs Phelps embodies the banality of racism: her cruelty is casual and habitual, showing that the system did not require deliberate malice to destroy lives.

lessons.title: Staging, Structure & Historical Drama
lessons.description: Multi-scene structure, songs, dual timeline, and Gupta's choices as a historical dramatist.
lessons.content_html:
Gupta’s Dramatic Choices

For the Edexcel exam, you are assessed on your ability to analyse how a playwright uses language, form, and structure to create meaning (AO1). This lesson focuses on the dramatic choices Gupta makes in The Empress — how the play is structured, how it uses music and song, how it handles the relationship between historical fact and dramatic fiction, and how its staging communicates theme.

Multi-Scene Structure

Unlike plays that follow a single continuous storyline, The Empress uses an episodic structure with multiple short scenes set in different locations and following different characters. This structure allows Gupta to weave together the stories of the ayahs, lascars, and political figures, creating a broad panoramic view of the Indian experience in Victorian Britain.

The episodic structure has several dramatic effects. First, it prevents the audience from settling into one character’s perspective, forcing them to see exploitation from multiple angles. Second, it mirrors the fragmented nature of the historical record — the stories of Indian people in Victorian Britain survive only in scattered documents, not in a single coherent narrative. Third, it creates pace and energy, moving between intimate personal moments and broader political scenes.

Key Fact

Gupta’s episodic structure serves her political purpose. By showing many characters in many situations, she demonstrates that exploitation was systemic — not the misfortune of one individual but the deliberate product of an entire system. The structure is the argument.

Songs and Music

The Empress incorporates songs and music as integral elements of the drama, not just background decoration. Indian music and song interrupt the naturalistic action, creating moments of beauty, community, and cultural identity that stand in contrast to the exploitation the characters face. The songs serve multiple purposes: they express emotions that dialogue cannot fully capture, they assert Indian cultural identity in a hostile environment, and they create a sense of communal solidarity among the Indian characters.

Music in The Empress functions as an act of resistance. In a society that views Indian culture as inferior, the characters’ songs assert the beauty and value of their heritage. The music also disrupts the play’s naturalistic naturalism, reminding the audience that they are watching a constructed drama, not a documentary. This Brechtian effect encourages the audience to think critically about what they are seeing rather than simply feeling sympathy.

The contrast between the beauty of the music and the ugliness of the exploitation is itself a dramatic device. It shows the audience what the characters have — rich cultural traditions, artistic expression, communal bonds — alongside what the Empire takes away.

The Dual Timeline

Gupta structures the play across a dual timeline, moving between different periods in the 1880s and 1890s. This technique allows her to show how exploitation evolved and persisted over time, and to juxtapose early hope with later disillusionment. The dual timeline also enables Gupta to incorporate real historical events — like Naoroji’s 1892 election — alongside fictional personal stories.

The movement between timelines creates dramatic irony. When the audience sees characters in the earlier timeline making hopeful plans, they already know (from scenes set later) how those plans will be thwarted. This structural technique reinforces the play’s theme that the Empire’s promises are consistently broken.

Key Fact

The dual timeline creates structural dramatic irony. The audience holds two time periods simultaneously — seeing hope in one and its destruction in the other. This technique turns the audience into witnesses who understand the full scope of the characters’ experience, even when the characters themselves do not.

Historical vs. Fictional Characters

One of Gupta’s most important dramatic choices is blending real historical figures (Dadabhai Naoroji, Queen Victoria as an offstage presence) with fictional characters (Rani, Abdul, Hari). This technique gives the play both historical authority and emotional intimacy. The historical figures ground the play in verifiable fact, while the fictional characters allow Gupta to explore personal emotions and experiences that the historical record does not capture.

The Empress belongs to the genre of historical drama. This genre gives Gupta the freedom to imagine the inner lives of people whose stories were not recorded while maintaining the historical framework that makes the play’s political argument credible. The fictional characters represent the thousands of unnamed ayahs and lascars whose stories were lost.

The blend also allows Gupta to control the audience’s response. Historical facts (like Naoroji’s election) provide moments of hope, while fictional experiences (like Rani’s abandonment) provide moments of emotional devastation. Together, they create the play’s distinctive tone of hope mixed with disillusionment.

Staging and Space

The original RSC production of The Empress used a relatively bare stage that transformed between locations through lighting, props, and the actors’ movements. This minimal staging keeps the focus on the characters and their stories rather than spectacle. It also reflects the characters’ displacement — they are people without a secure home, moving through spaces that belong to others.

Gupta’s staging choices communicate theme. The contrast between the cramped, dark spaces where Indian characters live and the implied grandeur of the Empire (referenced but never shown) visualises the power imbalance at the heart of the play. The absence of elaborate scenery mirrors the absence of support that Indian immigrants experienced in Victorian Britain.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Structure and staging questions are common in Edexcel Component 1. When writing about dramatic choices, always explain the effect on the audience. Don’t just identify a technique (“Gupta uses an episodic structure”) — analyse why (“the episodic structure forces the audience to see exploitation from multiple perspectives, making the systemic argument inescapable”). Link form to meaning.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The episodic structure shows exploitation from multiple perspectives, proving it is systemic rather than individual.
  • Songs and music function as acts of cultural resistance and create Brechtian disruption, encouraging critical thinking.
  • The blend of historical and fictional characters gives the play both factual authority and emotional intimacy, allowing Gupta to recover stories that the historical record erased.

lessons.title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
lessons.description: Empire, identity, racism, gender, and resistance explored with exam technique for Edexcel essays.
lessons.content_html:
The Play’s Key Themes

The Empress explores several interconnected themes, all of which relate to the experience of Indian people in Victorian Britain. For the exam, you need to be able to write about themes with precision — not just naming them but analysing how Gupta develops them through character, structure, and language. This lesson examines the five central themes and provides exam technique for writing strong essay responses.

Empire and Exploitation

The dominant theme of the play is the exploitation that underpinned the British Empire. Gupta shows that the Empire was not a benevolent force bringing civilisation to the world, but a system designed to extract wealth and labour from colonised people. Every character’s suffering in the play can be traced back to the structures of Empire: the ayahs are abandoned because the system treats them as disposable; the lascars are exploited because colonial laws protect British interests, not Indian workers; political progress is resisted because the Empire depends on racial hierarchy.

Key Fact

Gupta presents the British Empire as a system of exploitation, not a civilising mission. Every form of suffering in the play — abandonment, racial abuse, legal inequality, political exclusion — is shown to be a product of imperial structures, not individual cruelty.

Identity and Belonging

The Indian characters in the play face a constant crisis of identity. They are caught between two worlds: India, where they have cultural roots but limited economic opportunity, and Britain, where they can find work but are denied belonging. Gupta explores how the Empire forced Indian people to navigate a society that simultaneously needed their labour and rejected their presence.

The songs and cultural practices in the play represent the characters’ attempts to maintain their Indian identity in a hostile environment. When the ayahs sing together or share food, they create small spaces of belonging within a system designed to make them feel alien. Gupta suggests that cultural identity is a form of resistance — holding onto who you are when the world tells you that you are worth less.

Gupta deliberately connects the Victorian experience of exclusion to modern debates about immigration and belonging. The characters’ struggle to be accepted in Britain despite contributing to its economy mirrors the experiences of immigrant communities today. This connection is central to AO3 — understanding how the play’s meaning is shaped by the context in which Gupta wrote it (2013, during intense political debate about immigration in Britain).

The play argues that belonging should not depend on race or origin — the Indian characters contribute to British society through their labour, their culture, and their political participation. Gupta challenges the idea that Britishness is defined by whiteness, a challenge that remains relevant today.

Racism

Racism in The Empress operates on multiple levels. There is the overt racism of Lord Salisbury, who mocks Naoroji as “a black man.” There is the casual racism of Mrs Phelps, who treats Indian servants as inferior without conscious malice. And there is structural racism — the legal and economic systems that pay Indian workers less, deny them legal protection, and allow employers to abandon them without consequence.

Key Fact

Gupta shows racism operating on three levels: overt hostility (Salisbury), casual condescension (Mrs Phelps), and structural inequality (laws and economic systems). By showing all three, she argues that racism is not just about individual attitudes but about how entire systems are designed to maintain racial hierarchy.

Gender

The play explores how gender intersects with race to create different forms of exploitation. The ayahs face specific gendered vulnerabilities: they are employed as carers for children (traditionally female work), they are more economically dependent on their employers, and they face the additional danger of being women alone in a foreign country. Gupta shows that Indian women faced a double burden — exploited both for their race and their gender.

At the same time, Gupta presents the ayahs as sources of strength, not just victims of oppression. Their solidarity, their care for each other, and their cultural practices represent a form of resistance that is specifically female. Rani’s resilience is shaped by her identity as a woman — she endures, adapts, and protects others in ways that the male characters do not always manage.

Resistance and Agency

The final major theme is agency — the characters’ ability to resist and act despite the system that oppresses them. Gupta presents resistance in many forms: Hari’s political anger, Naoroji’s electoral success, the ayahs’ mutual support, Rani’s refusal to be broken. The play argues that even within systems of extreme oppression, people find ways to assert their humanity and fight for justice.

Essay questions on this play typically give you a quotation from the play and ask you to write an extended response. You must cover the whole play, not just the quotation. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact format and mark weightings. Here is a strong paragraph structure:

Point: Make a clear argument about how Gupta presents the theme or character. Evidence: Use a quotation or specific moment from the play. Analysis: Analyse language, structure, or dramatic choices (AO1). Context: Connect to historical or social context (AO3). Evaluation: Offer an alternative interpretation or evaluate the effect on the audience.

Strong phrases for evaluation: “An alternative reading is that…” / “A contemporary audience might interpret this as…” / “While one perspective suggests… it could equally be argued that…” / “Gupta’s deliberate ambiguity invites the audience to consider whether…”

Plan before you write. Identify the key theme or character the question targets, choose 3–4 moments from across the play (not just one act), and decide your overall argument. Aim for 4–5 paragraphs, each following the Point-Evidence-Analysis-Context-Evaluation structure. Reserve a few minutes at the end to check your spelling, punctuation, and grammar.

The most common mistake is writing about only one part of the play. Examiners reward responses that range across the whole text, showing how themes develop from Act 1 through to the ending. Plan your paragraphs to cover different acts or different characters to demonstrate breadth.

Gupta’s play is ultimately about power — who has it, who lacks it, and what happens when the powerless refuse to accept their position. Every theme in the play connects back to this central question: can a system built on exploitation ever be reformed, or must it be dismantled entirely?
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Edexcel AO4, you must evaluate and offer alternative interpretations. Practise this by taking each theme and arguing two opposing positions. For example: “The play ultimately argues that resistance is futile because the system is too powerful” versus “The play argues that every act of resistance has value, even if the system remains.” The best answers hold both positions and explain why Gupta leaves the question open.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five central themes — empire and exploitation, identity and belonging, racism, gender, and resistance — are all interconnected and should be discussed in relation to each other.
  • Racism operates on three levels in the play: overt, casual, and structural. Showing awareness of all three demonstrates sophisticated analysis.
  • For the Edexcel essay, use the Point-Evidence-Analysis-Context-Evaluation structure, cover the whole play, and always offer alternative interpretations for AO4.
